summary: This program is the driver for a small bakery model: it builds one plain cookie and one decorated cookie, then asks each object to describe itself. It shows how a program that holds `main` can stay short by letting the objects do the work.

lines.text: This class exists only to run the program, so it holds no cookie data of its own. Keeping the driver separate from `Cookie` and `DecoratedCookie` is a common way to organise Java code.
Java starts every program at `main`, which is why this method must be `public static void` with a `String[]` parameter.
`new Cookie(...)` builds one object in memory and hands the flavour to the constructor; `regular` is the variable that lets you reach that object later.
A `DecoratedCookie` is a specialised kind of cookie, so it is created the same way but carries extra information about its decoration.
Calling `describe()` asks the object itself to produce its own description, rather than having `main` assemble the text from separate fields.
The same method name works on the decorated cookie, but the subclass's own version runs and mentions the decoration — this is polymorphism in action.
